notes: \cpara{Links to the previous post and states the young author's refusal to define intelligence: not mathematically, and, the post adds, hardly at all.}

\cfact{The archived early texts do define intelligence, informally. ``Staring into the Singularity'' (text dated 1996 and 1999) has a section headed ``The Definition of Smartness'': ``Smartness is the measure of what you see as obvious, what you can see as obvious in retrospect, what you can invent, and what you can comprehend.'' ``The Plan to Singularity'' (1999--2000) says: ``Intelligence is whatever lets you model, predict, and manipulate reality.'' Neither is mathematical, so the first sentence stands. ``Any definition \ldots\ at all,'' and ``I refused to define it at all'' in the third paragraph, are stronger than the record; the post's later wording, ``not to precisely define,'' fits it.}

\cpara{Gives the young author's reason: in AI, a loose definition of intelligence invites a cheap program that meets the definition and is then announced as intelligence. The examples are types of system, not named projects.}

\cpara{Diagnoses the refusal as an overreaction to other people's mistakes, the pattern of ``Reversed Stupidity Is Not Intelligence'' in Book II, and names the young author's real target: something ``powerful enough to take stars apart for raw material.''}

\cpara{Gives a second overreaction: because neat math had kept AI projects on toy problems, the young author doubted any neat math of intelligence, ``Except for Bayes's Theorem.'' I could not reach ``Coding a Transhuman AI,'' the likeliest place for that exception, so it is unchecked; the other early texts I read do not mention Bayes.}
\cpara{Offers, with ``it's hard for me to remember,'' a root cause: too few AI books, too popular, and the wrong ones.}

\cpara{Adds that the young author had written AI off as a ``sick, dead field'' that had not delivered on its promises. ``The Plan to Singularity'' (1999--2000) bears this out: ``The research talent we need is more likely to reside in the field now called `cognitive science' than in the field called AI. AI remains crippled by the ideologies formed back when it was necessary to believe that a 50's-era computer program was exhibiting `intelligence'.''}
\cpara{States the thesis: the same belief was one of the author's best and one of the worst mistakes.}
\cpara{Explains the ``best'' half: expecting no simple answer, the young author read widely and did not stop at the first bright idea.}

\cpara{Grants both errors, and credits neuroanatomy with the idea that a mind divides into parts like ``visual cortex,'' not ``commonsense reasoning module.'' ``The Plan to Singularity'' shows the idea in use: it calls a module for source code a ``codic cortex,'' ``by analogy to the human `visual cortex'.''}

\cfact{The post does not say here which mathematics it means; ``My Bayesian Enlightenment,'' later in this sequence, takes that up. Formal work of this kind had appeared the year before the post: Legg and Hutter's ``Universal Intelligence: A Definition of Machine Intelligence'' (arXiv, 2007) gives a formal definition, starting from the remark that ``nobody really knows what intelligence is.'' Hutter's 2005 book is cited in the introduction to this book.}
\cpara{Restates the point of the last paragraph in general form.}
\cpara{Turns from the reasons to what the belief led the young author to do.}
\cpara{First consequence: study of the cognitive sciences.}
\cpara{Second consequence: not stopping at one brilliant idea.}
\cpara{Third consequence: long study before proposing any system, the practice recommended in ``Hold Off On Proposing Solutions.''}
\cpara{Sums up the ``best'' half.}
\cpara{Introduces the moral.}
\cpara{The moral, in the book's term ``screens off'': once you know what someone did, the reason they had adds nothing to what you can predict about the result.}
\cpara{Applies the moral: of two clever arguments that may both prove wrong, the one that leads you to study more leaves you better placed.}

\cpara{Admits luck: many successes were right actions for wrong reasons. The ``anthropic principle'' remark is a selection effect turned against the author's own record: readers hear only from the author who did not reach a dead end. The stated purpose of the writing, to leave a trail to where the author ended up by accident, matches what the introduction to this book says about why the essays were written.}
\cpara{Gives the ``worst'' half: informality meant low standards, and the clever reason for not defining intelligence precisely let sloppy reasoning in.}

\cpara{Answers that defining intelligence at once would also have been wrong, since a right definition needs knowledge the young author lacked. This keeps the refusal to define; the mistake, as the next paragraph says, lay elsewhere.}
\cpara{The rule, by analogy with fire before atoms were known: informal talk is needed to investigate, but conclusions drawn at that level must not be trusted.}

\cpara{Ends with a metaphor for trusting such a conclusion, and a promise to continue. Which conclusion is not said here. ``A Prodigy of Refutation,'' two posts on, returns to the young author's belief that a superintelligence ``will also know what's right far better than a human being could.''}
